item.title: Ritzy Miami steakhouse manager held on ICE detainer after mom found stabbed to death
item.description: Surveillance video allegedly shows the Miami steakhouse manager blood-soaked in an elevator with a knife hours after returning home with his mother.
item.content:encoded:
A Miami steakhouse manager allegedly emerged from his luxury apartment covered in blood and clutching a knife before telling police he had acted in self-defense after his mother was found stabbed to death inside.

Stefano Eduardo Cremasco-Cicero, 36, told officers, "I was defending myself," after Miami police were called to the Brickell high-rise early Friday, according to an arrest report obtained by WPLG.

Cremasco-Cicero is charged with second-degree murder with a weapon, Miami-Dade County jail records show.

KARMELO ANTHONY STAYS SILENT AS ANALYSTS WARN DEFENSE FACES UPHILL BATTLE IN TRACK MEET STABBING TRIAL

Officers were dispatched at about 4:47 a.m. for an "unknown request for police assistance," according to the outlet.

Officers found Cremasco-Cicero in the lobby with blood on his hands, clothing and shoes, the outlet reported.

He allegedly directed officers upstairs to the apartment.

Inside the apartment, police found his mother lying behind the front door with multiple apparent stab wounds, according to WPLG. Miami Fire Rescue pronounced her dead shortly after 5 a.m.

FLORIDA MAN ACCUSED OF KILLING MOM AND BURNING BODY BECAUSE SHE ‘WANTED TO BE CREMATED’

Authorities have not publicly identified the woman or disclosed her age. Police said she was visiting from Mexico and staying with her son.

The unusual chain of events began when a food delivery driver arrived at the building and encountered Cremasco-Cicero in the lobby, according to the report.

He allegedly opened the door for the driver and asked her to call 911. Cremasco-Cicero ultimately placed the call himself but handed the phone to the woman so she could give the dispatcher the building information, WPLG reported.

The driver noticed blood on him as they waited for police, according to the outlet. When she tried to return his phone, he allegedly refused to take it, and she later handed it to responding officers.

THE SURVEILLANCE CAMERA ON YOUR STREET CORNER: LAWFUL SPYING OR CONSTITUTIONALLY PROBLEMATIC?

Investigators then turned to surveillance video and building access records to piece together what happened in the hours before police arrived.

Surveillance video showed Cremasco-Cicero and his mother returning to the building together at about 10:32 p.m. Thursday, according to WPLG. They were reportedly alone in the elevator.

COURTNEY CLENNEY'S DEFENSE INSPECTS KNIVES AT CENTER OF ONLYFANS MODEL'S MURDER CASE AHEAD OF TRIAL: REPORT

At about 4:26 a.m., surveillance video allegedly captured Cremasco-Cicero entering an elevator wearing a white shirt, khaki pants and white shoes that appeared to be covered in blood. Police said he was carrying a knife.

He allegedly dropped the knife after stepping out of the elevator, picked it back up and rode another elevator upstairs, according to the report.

Investigators said Cremasco-Cicero later reappeared in a different, long-sleeved blue shirt and walked out of the building while using his phone. He returned minutes later and sat on a couch in the lobby before flagging down the delivery driver, WPLG reported.

Police said Cremasco-Cicero had small cuts on his hands and blood residue on his body and clothing. Crime scene investigators photographed him and collected his clothes, according to the outlet.

5 REASONS MORE AMERICANS ARE CUTTING OFF THEIR OWN PARENTS, ACCORDING TO PSYCHOLOGIST

After obtaining a search warrant, homicide detectives allegedly recovered several kitchen knives with blood on them, blood-spattered shirts, broken glass and a broken wine bottle from the apartment, WPLG reported.

Cremasco-Cicero’s wife told detectives she was in France attending a wedding when the killing happened, according to the report. She said her husband and his mother had not been close since his parents divorced and that he had recently been under stress while preparing to open a restaurant in Coconut Grove.

The Miami Herald identified Cremasco-Cicero as the U.S. operating manager of the high-end 1986 Steakhouse in Miami.

The arrest report identified Cremasco-Cicero as a Miami resident through an investor visa, according to WPLG.

Miami-Dade Corrections records reviewed by Fox News Digital show Cremasco-Cicero was booked Friday night and is being held at the Turner Guilford Knight Correctional Center. The records list no bond, a domestic-violence designation and a hold for immigration authorities.

The jail record does not provide additional details about the immigration hold.

A Department of Homeland Security spokesperson confirmed to Fox News Digital that Cremasco-Cicero is an illegal immigrant.

"On August 5, 2026, ICE lodged a detainer for Stefano Eduardo Cremasco Cicero, a criminal illegal alien from Mexico, charged with homicide," the DHS spokesperson said. "We are calling on Florida to honor our detainer. His claims will be heard by an immigration judge and he will receive due process. This administration will not ignore the rule of law."

"Under President Trump and Secretary Mullin, if you break the law, you will face the consequences," the spokesperson added. "Criminal illegal aliens are not welcome in the U.S."

A motive for the killing remains unclear.

Fox News Digital reached out to the Miami Police Department, the Miami-Dade Clerk of Courts and 1986 Steakhouse for additional information.

item.title: Rob Lowe says Tom Cruise was his ‘nemesis’ in the fight for blockbuster roles
item.description: Rob Lowe reveals Tom Cruise repeatedly beat him out for iconic roles like "Top Gun" and "Jerry Maguire" during their early Hollywood careers.
item.content:encoded:
Rob Lowe had plenty of competition for blockbuster roles in the 1980s and ’90s – and one Hollywood heavyweight repeatedly stood in his way.

"That dastardly Tom Cruise was always a nemesis," Lowe told the New York Post.

"I remember reading ‘Jerry Maguire’ ... and they were like, ‘Tom Cruise.’ I also remember reading ‘Top Gun’ and going, ‘Oh, this movie is going to be f---ing massive,'" he recalled. "They were like, ‘Tom Cruise.'"

'BLUE LAGOON' STAR CHRISTOPHER ATKINS SAYS ALCOHOL COST HIM ICONIC 'FOOTLOOSE' ROLE BEFORE GETTING SOBER

Despite losing out on what he considered to be big roles. Lowe found his stride as a core member of the Brat Pack. He starred in several career-defining films of the Brat Pack-era, including "St. Elmo's Fire," "The Outsiders," "Class" and "Oxford Blues."

Yet one major piece was missing from Lowe’s ’80s résumé – a coveted role in a John Hughes movie.

Lowe admitted he was never in the running for the coming-of-age hit "Ferris Bueller’s Day Off."

"No, that’s a big regret," he said, noting Hughes was not interested in casting Lowe for the role that went to Matthew Broderick.

"John Hughes never got what I was selling," Lowe explained.

"I met with John once, and it’s not like he didn’t have a lot of parts I could have done," he added. "When you really look at it, there were more than a few parts, multiple parts in some movies. Never, phone never rang."

Decades later, Lowe has come up with his own explanation for why Hughes never came calling.

"I have a theory about it; I think I was actually already too well known," Lowe said.

"John put in people who [weren’t] already well known," he explained. "He made people well known. At least that’s what I tell myself to make myself feel better for not getting a role in ‘The Breakfast Club.'"

Lowe's early movie roles established him as a teen heartthrob, but he later built a remarkably durable career spanning film, network television and streaming projects.

A major second act came with his role as Sam Seaborn on "The West Wing," which earned him Emmy and Golden Globe nominations. He later showed off his comedic side as the relentlessly upbeat Chris Traeger on "Parks and Recreation."

item.title: Judge denies ousted Stars and Stripes journalists effort to reverse Pentagon's firings
item.description: A federal judge denied fired Stars and Stripes journalists' bid for a restraining order, but the trio says the Pentagon press freedom fight isn't over.
item.content:encoded:
A federal judge Friday denied a request from the trio of ousted Stars and Stripes journalists to reverse the Pentagon's firing of them.

U.S. District Judge Trevor McFadden denied a temporary restraining order filed by Stars and Stripes publisher Max Lederer, editor in chief Erik Slavin and reporter Lara Korte, claiming they "ultimately fail to carry their significant burden to show that they are clearly entitled to a preliminary injunction."

In a joint statement to Fox News Digital, the three journalists expressed their disappointment with McFadden's decision but insist it's not the "final judgment."

"We are reviewing the decision with our attorneys and considering our next steps," Lederer, Slavin and Korte said. "We continue to believe that the Pentagon should not be able to fire journalists for speaking out against censorship and defending the editorial independence of Stars and Stripes."

FIRED STARS AND STRIPES SUE PENTAGON, ALLEGE RETALIATION AND FIRST AMENDMENT VIOLATION

"This case is not primarily about the three of us. It is about whether the servicemembers who swear to defend the Constitution, and the military families who serve alongside them, can rely on a free and independent press. It is also about whether the military and civilian journalists at Stars and Stripes can do their jobs without fear of retaliation," they added.

Chief Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell touted the legal win on social media.

"The court applied settled Supreme Court law: public employees do not receive First Amendment protection when they speak with the government’s voice," Parnell wrote on X. "The record showed these interviews were arranged with supervisor involvement, conducted at Stripes workplaces, and presented the speakers in their official titles, discussing the paper they run. That is government speech, not private-citizen speech."

"Stars and Stripes is a Department of War publication funded to inform the military community," Parnell continued. "The Department has both the authority and the responsibility to ensure it remains focused on the force — warfighting, readiness, and the men and women who serve — rather than becoming a platform for airing employee grievances. We will follow the law and complete the personnel process."

TRUMP ADMINISTRATION SUBPOENAS NY TIMES JOURNALISTS IN GRAND JURY LEAK PROBE TIED TO AIR FORCE ONE REPORT

Last month, the Pentagon fired the journalists from the military newspaper over alleged insubordination. In return, they filed a lawsuit alleging retaliation and violation of their First Amendment rights.

The firings stem from Slavin and Korte's unauthorized participation in a July "CBS Sunday Morning" segment about the Pentagon's efforts to overhaul the paper and Lederer's refusal to fire them at the direction of Pentagon leadership.

According to the lawsuit, the trio allege Pentagon leadership "understood these interview statements expressed personal opinions, and therefore took no immediate action, despite their displeasure" and that it wasn't until Stars and Stripes published its report on the alleged strife aboard USS Abraham Lincoln that the Pentagon's stance had shifted.

The lawsuit notes that Pentagon leadership demanded Lederer to fire Slavin and Korte just one day after the report was published.

Listed as the defendants in the lawsuit are the Pentagon, Secretary of War Pete Hegseth, Parnell and his principal deputy assistant, Andrew Brey.

In an interview with Fox News Digital, Slavin insisted the Pentagon never explicitly stated how he and Korte were deemed insubordinate for the CBS News interview, noting that he had given many other media interviews without having to seek authorization from Pentagon leadership.

"This isn't about me. It's not about three jobs. It's about whether servicemembers and their families are gonna have access to independent news and information and news that they can trust," Slavin said. "And it's my concern for our staff that they might face further retaliation if they make statements along the lines of 'Hey, we work for Stars and Stripes and we provide independent news.' So this is about protecting an institution, in my mind."

item.title: Dangerous mosquito-borne virus spreads in one state as officials warn of rising cases
item.description: Florida dengue fever cases hit 41 statewide as mosquito-control crews ramp up aerial spraying and inspections across Tampa Bay's hardest-hit counties.
item.content:encoded:
Florida mosquito-control agencies are stepping up surveillance, inspections and spraying, as officials expect the number of locally acquired dengue fever cases in Tampa Bay and across the state to rise in the coming weeks.

As of Sept. 1, the number of dengue fever cases originating in Florida this year had climbed to 33 in Tampa Bay and 41 statewide. Cases are predicted to increase, Fox 13 Tampa Bay reported.

Locally acquired cases mean people contracted the illness where they live rather than while traveling abroad.

DEADLY MOSQUITO-BORNE VIRUS CLAIMS FIRST LIFE IN MAJOR US CITY AS CASES SPREAD

The Florida Mosquito Control Association (FMCA) reported 30 confirmed cases in Hillsborough County, seven in Miami-Dade County, three in Pinellas County and one in Palm Beach County.

Hillsborough and Pinellas counties are under mosquito-borne illness alerts issued by the Florida Department of Health.

Dengue is a mosquito-borne viral illness that can cause fever, severe aches, nausea, rash and, in rare cases, life-threatening complications, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.

The virus is most prevalent in tropical and subtropical regions, including Southeast Asia, the Western Pacific islands, Latin America and Africa. Though less common in the continental U.S., locally acquired cases have been recorded in Florida, California and Texas.

Hawaii has recorded past outbreaks, and the virus is common in the U.S. territories of Puerto Rico, the U.S. Virgin Islands and American Samoa.

The CDC reported in May that 2024 was a record year for dengue in the U.S.

A total of 3,798 cases were reported from U.S. states and the District of Columbia, a 359% increase over the annual average for 2010 through 2023. About 97% of those cases were travel-associated, and roughly 3% were locally acquired.

Florida reported the most dengue cases among U.S. states and Washington, D.C., in 2024, with 1,044 cases, or more than a quarter of the total. Florida recorded 85 locally acquired cases across 10 counties that year, compared with 18 in California and two in Texas.

TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"Dengue does not stop at county lines," Pinellas County Mosquito Control Director Alissa Berro told Fox 13.

"The mosquitoes that transmit the virus generally stay within a relatively small area, but people travel throughout the Tampa Bay area every day. When someone infected with dengue enters a new area, a local mosquito can bite that person and later spread the virus to others. As cases rise across the region, so does the potential for additional local transmission."

Mosquito-control crews in Florida are increasing aerial and ground treatments in areas showing dengue virus activity, while also inspecting private properties for potential mosquito breeding sites, according to local reports.

FMCA is urging residents to empty or cover standing water around their homes. The mosquito that spreads dengue is a container breeder, meaning it lays eggs in buckets, planters, plant saucers, tires, discarded toys and other objects that collect small amounts of water, experts say.

CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR LIFESTYLE NEWSLETTER

The FMCA also advises people to follow what it calls the "three Ds."

Many people infected with dengue have no symptoms, and most people who do become sick recover within a week or two, according to Mayo Clinic.

In some cases, however, the illness can progress to severe dengue, a potentially life-threatening condition.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE LIFESTYLE NEWS

Warning signs can develop quickly, often within a day or two after the fever subsides. Those may include severe stomach pain, repeated vomiting, unusual bleeding or bruising, difficulty breathing, extreme tiredness and irritability, or restlessness. 

People experiencing warning signs of severe dengue should seek immediate medical care.

item.title: Michigan coach says Bryce Underwood is Wolverines quarterback for 'right now' after near disaster in opener
item.description: Kyle Whittingham says Bryce Underwood's spot atop Michigan football's depth chart is "not something that's infinite" after the narrow victory.
item.content:encoded:
Heading into the college football season, there was not a single person who would have predicted that Michigan quarterback Bryce Underwood would be put on notice after the Wolverines' season opener against Western Michigan, yet here we are.

Michigan avoided what would have been one of the most embarrassing losses in program history to the directional school after Bryce Underwood connected with wide receiver JJ Buchanan on a Hail Mary for a 13-12 victory. Underwood sailed his first Hail Mary attempt out of the back of the end zone, and despite the clock appearing to hit triple zeros to end the game, officials added one second back onto the clock after a review, which led to Underwood's heroics.

While Underwood's perfect pass to Buchanan saved the day, and perhaps the entire year for Michigan, that doesn't mean he's earned an infinite leash as QB1 in head coach Kyle Whittingham's eyes.

MICHIGAN FANS CALLED OUT ON SOCIAL MEDIA FOR RUSHING FIELD AFTER WOLVERINES STEAL WIN OVER WESTERN MICHIGAN

"He's our QB right now, it's not something that's infinite," Whittingham told reporters on Monday. "At some point, we've got to turn a corner, and we've got to see improvement.

"As we do with a bunch of stuff, we've got to see improvement out of the coaches. It's not just Bryce; it's not just Bryce's job that is not absolutely set in concrete. Nobody's is, you've got to perform week in and week out. Become somebody that we feel is playing at a level that we can win with."

Whittingham pointing a finger at himself and his coaching staff after the near-nightmare start to the season is certainly valid, but him specifically stating that Underwood's name being atop the depth chart is "not something that's infinite" is certainly noteworthy.

The sophomore signal caller signed a historic NIL deal worth a reported $12 million upon joining the Wolverines as the top quarterback in the 2025 class. Potentially benching a quarterback being paid $4 million per year would fall into the easier-said-than-done category, but Whittingham is, at the very least, willing to send a message to his young QB through the media.

Underwood threw for 170 yards and rushed for another 47 yards and accounted for both of Michigan's touchdowns against the Broncos while also throwing one interception.

The Michigan native threw 11 touchdowns and nine interceptions as a freshman with the Wolverines a season ago.

item.title: 'Happy Days' star Linda Purl steps out in Los Angeles during 71st birthday week
item.description: Linda Purl celebrated her 71st birthday last week while juggling a new album, an off-Broadway play directed by former "Happy Days" costar Anson Williams and much more.
item.content:encoded:
Linda Purl was spotted this week picking up a cake and groceries from a Gelson’s market in Los Angeles.

The "Happy Days" star turned 71 years old on Wednesday.

Purl played Henry Winkler's character Fonzie’s fiancée, single mom Ashley Pfister, during the 1970s and ‘80s sitcom’s second-to-last season. She also played a different character who occasionally dated Richie Cunningham, played by Ron Howard, in the show’s second season.

'HAPPY DAYS' STAR SCOTT BAIO SAYS HE WAS ALMOST FIRED FROM ICONIC SERIES AFTER 'GETTING A BIG HEAD'

Purl also played Andy Griffith’s daughter on "Matlock" in the 1980s and Pam Beesley’s mother who briefly dated Michael Scott.

The seasoned actress, who has been in a relationship with "Dallas" star Patrick Duffy for six years, kept it casual as she shopped, wearing a red baseball cap, long-sleeve blue top and black pants.

'HAPPY DAYS' STAR HENRY WINKLER FILMED HIS FIRST-EVER NUDE SCENE AT 79

The couple have been together since 2020, when they reconnected during the pandemic.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

Purl continues to act with roles on "General Hospital," "The Bold and the Beautiful," "After Forever" and the movie "Hollywood Grit," which she stars in alongside Duffy and Tyrese Gibson, in the last few years.

DAVID FOSTER HELPED LAUNCH HER MUSIC CAREER IN HER 70S — NOW SHE HAS 60 MILLION STREAMS

The actress, who is also a singer, just released a new album this summer, "From My Heart," which is a mix of Great American Songbook classics and jazz, and she’s starring in an off-Broadway one-woman play this month called "Crazy Mama."

The show, playing on 59th Street in Manhattan, is directed by Purl’s former "Happy Days" costar Anson Williams, who played Potsie on the show. The show was written by Anson’s wife, Sharon Scott Williams.

HENRY WINKLER OPENS UP ABOUT THE UNEXPECTED CAREER HE CONSIDERED BEFORE BECOMING AN ACTOR

"The play is directed by my dear friend of many decades now, fellow actor, Anson Williams," she told BroadwayWorld. "We first met when we working together on Happy Days. At the time, we thought we were just young kids bouncing off to a swell place to work. Little did we know that we also were planting seeds that would come to new fruition this far into our lives."

She also talked about the sourdough bread company that she started six years ago with Duffy.

'GOD BLESS THE USA' STAR REVIVES PATRIOTIC SPIRITS BRAND BENEFITING VETERANS FOR AMERICA'S 250TH BIRTHDAY

"Right from the get-go we wanted all of our profits to go to food scarcity efforts," she explained. "Think, Newman‘s Own wannabes. It was a terrible business model because once you buy a sourdough starter, which is what we were selling, you never have to buy it again, so we knew we had to find somebody who’d take us on, bake the bread and distribute it."

For the last year, she said she and Duffy have been traveling around to Kroger stores across the country sharing their bread.

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"We just passed the 2,300 stores mark," she boasted. "All the years we were working out of the garage we managed to give away a whopping $250. Since going with Kroger, I am astonished to say that along with them we have just passed the 200K amount in support to food scarcity efforts. It’s a drop in the bucket, but the statistics on hunger in America are staggering, so we’ll plug along as long as Kroger will have us. It has been an adventure to say the least."

She told Fox News Digital in 2022 that "Happy Days" was one of her first jobs in Los Angeles.

‘BEWITCHED’ ACTRESS ERIN MURPHY REUNITES WITH FORMER CHILD STARS IN NOSTALGIC HOLLYWOOD PHOTO

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"I went in, I auditioned, and I happened to get the role," she said of her season two stint on the show. "I came back many years later as an entirely different character. That came about because there was a casting notice [saying] they were looking for ‘a Linda Purl type.’ My agent called and said, ‘Do you think Linda could audition for this Linda Purl type?’ And I did. And thank heavens I got the role. Otherwise, I think I would’ve gone into some kind of identity crisis."

‘BRADY BUNCH’ CAST MADE NEARLY NOTHING FROM DECADES OF RERUNS, EVE PLUMB CLAIMS

Purl said "everything about that set was fun. The regular cast members were all friends and they’ve remained lifelong friends… We are a tight bunch."

She added, "There was an atmosphere on the set of ‘Happy Days’ where, when you opened the door to that sound stage on the Paramount lot, you would just leave your [troubles] behind and come into this kind of bubble, a world where things were sweet, light and joyful… I think all of that feel-good vibe came into the performances that we were able to do."

Fox News' Stephanie Nolasco contributed to this report.

item.title: Two men die within 24 hours at Burning Man as tens of thousands gather in the Nevada desert
item.description: Craigh Mann, 60, was found dead by campmates at Burning Man on Saturday, just one day after another participant suffered a fatal medical emergency.
item.content:encoded:
Two men died within roughly 24 hours at Burning Man as tens of thousands of "burners" gathered in the Nevada desert for the final days of the famed festival.

One of the men, identified as 60-year-old Craigh Mann, was found dead by campmates Saturday afternoon, festival organizers said. Another participant in his mid-50s died after suffering a medical emergency a day earlier.

Mann was found at his camp in Black Rock City at about 3 p.m. Saturday, Sept. 5, according to the Burning Man Project.

BURNING MAN MURDER MYSTERY DEEPENS AS NEW DETAILS EMERGE 1 YEAR AFTER DESERT FESTIVAL KILLING

"Burning Man Project is saddened to share that a second Black Rock City participant, Craigh Mann, a 60-year-old man, was found deceased by campmates in his camp," organizers said in a statement.

"Our thoughts and deepest condolences are with the participant’s family, friends, campmates, and all those affected by this loss," the statement said.

Festival organizers announced the first death Friday evening.

The man who was in his mid-50s suffered a medical emergency and received lifesaving measures before being taken to the festival’s onsite emergency care center, according to the Burning Man Project.

BURNING MAN HOMICIDE UNSOLVED AS WITNESS REPORTEDLY RECALLS CHILLING ENCOUNTER

He was pronounced dead at the center. Organizers did not provide further details about the type of medical emergency.

His name was not released because his family had not yet been notified.

"The safety and well-being of our community and staff remain our highest priority," organizers said after the first death. They said support resources were available around the clock for people in Black Rock City, the temporary city built each year to host the event.

The Pershing County Sheriff's Office did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

The annual Burning Man festival began Aug. 30 and was scheduled to conclude Monday.

The sprawling desert gathering draws as many as 80,000 people, known as "burners." The festival is best known for the burning of a large wooden effigy.

item.title: Police determine that a Maine Bigfoot was actually man in a 'very convincing costume'
item.description: Maine police launched a Bigfoot investigation after an unusually high number of sighting calls, only to find a man in a very convincing costume.
item.content:encoded:
Most Bigfoot mysteries go unsolved. There's either no evidence or evidence that isn't sufficient, like a blurry picture or a print in mud that sort of looks like an oversized foot.

This one is one of the ones that police were able to get to the bottom of. It started with several sightings being reported to the Damariscotta Police Department in Damariscotta, Maine last week.

Due to what the police department reported on Facebook were an "unusually high number of calls" they launched an investigation and determined that "Bigfoot is not real."

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS

I think what they meant to say is that this Bigfoot is not real. Perhaps that the supposed Bigfoot was wearing was a giveaway. An officer located the Bigfoot and, after a conversation, determined that it was a man in a costume.

Not just any costume, a "very convincing costume."

The police department took some positive aspects away from the investigation despite the disappointment that a hat wearing Bigfoot was nothing more than a man in a costume.

BIGFOOT HUNTER SUGGESTS THERE'S A CONSPIRACY AFTER CORNELL UNIVERSITY DENIES CONDUCTING DNA TESTS ON REMAINS

"We greatly appreciate everyone’s excitement, curiosity, and willingness to keep an eye out for one another," they wrote. "We also appreciate all the calls and information that came in. Rest assured, we were on the hunt from the very beginning."

A community coming together and looking out for one another. Maybe that's what Bigfoot has been trying to get across to us the entire time.

"While we didn't find Bigfoot, we did find something almost as rare: A town full of people willing to stop what they're doing to investigate a Bigfoot sighting and keep each other safe," the police department's post continued.

"And honestly, we wouldn't have it any other way."

They may not have had a Bigfoot wandering around their town and the several sightings turned out to be nothing, but the folks of Damariscotta have something more important than that.

They have one another.

item.title: Best outdoor adventures near DKR-Texas Memorial Stadium in Austin: Hiking, paddling and more for gameday
item.description: From Barton Springs Pool to Lake Travis ziplines, here are the best outdoor spots near DKR before Ohio State faces Texas in a primetime kickoff.
item.content:encoded:
Week 2 | Ohio State at Texas | Saturday, Sept. 12 | DKR-Texas Memorial Stadium, Austin, TX | 6:30 PM CT | ABC

Texas fans have seen this movie twice already and don't love the ending. Ohio State knocked the Longhorns out of the 2024 CFP in the Cotton Bowl semifinal, 28-14, on their way to that season's national title, then beat them again 14-7 in last year's season opener.

CLICK HERE FOR MORE COVERAGE FROM OUTKICK OUTDOORS

Now the preseason No. 1 Buckeyes are coming to Austin to face the No. 5 Longhorns for the latest installment, with "College GameDay" setting up on campus and a primetime kickoff on ABC. Arch Manning gets his shot at the rematch at home this time.

Whether that ends better for Texas or not, you'll have all day to burn off the nerves beforehand.

Austin doesn't require much of an excuse to get outside, and with a 6:30 kickoff, you've got a full day to work with before the stadium lights come on. From paddling downtown to ziplining over Lake Travis, here's where to go, all within an hour of DKR.

14 TAILGATING ESSENTIALS FOR GRILLING, WATCHING THE GAME AND STAYING WARM

A word on conditions: mid-September in Austin still runs hot, with highs typically in the low-to-mid 90s. Front-load anything exposed or physical into the morning and stay hydrated.

Under 10 minutes from DKR | ~$20-30/hour rental

About as close to the stadium as it gets. Rent a paddleboard or kayak from an outfitter like The Rowing Dock or Austin Paddle Shack and glide out onto calm, no-motorboats-allowed water with the downtown skyline as your backdrop — including a pass under the Congress Avenue Bridge, home to the city's famous bat colony.

About 10 minutes from DKR | Roughly $5-9 entry

The single best way to beat the heat on a 90-plus-degree gameday. This spring-fed pool inside Zilker Park holds a constant 68 degrees year-round, no matter how hot it gets outside. It's an Austin institution, so you can expect company. But it's worth the crowd.

BEST HIKING TRAILS NEAR SCOTT STADIUM IN CHARLOTTESVILLE: A GUIDE FOR VIRGINIA FOOTBALL FANS

About 15 minutes from DKR | Free

A steep but short climb — around 100 stairs — leads to a stunning overlook of the Colorado River, Lake Austin and the city skyline. There's essentially no shade at the top, so this is a morning or evening stop, not a 2 p.m. one.

15-20 minutes from DKR | Free

Austin's default answer for hiking and mountain biking, cutting through limestone canyon terrain right in the middle of the city. When water levels cooperate, several swimming holes open up along the trail, too.

About 20 minutes from DKR | Roughly $6 entry

Somehow this feels like a different state entirely despite being 20 minutes from downtown. Onion Creek's Upper and Lower Falls offer swimming holes and hiking trails that make you forget 100,000 people are about to pack into a stadium nearby.

25-35 minutes from DKR | $135/person for the full tour

This is the splurge pick. Five ziplines over roughly three hours, including Texas's longest line, plus a short hike and a boat ride built into the tour. If your crew wants one big memorable activity (and doesn't mind shelling out some dough), this is it.

Every week this season, OutKick OutDoors is finding the best ways to touch grass before you touch down at the tailgate. Got a favorite spot near your campus we should know about? Hit us up on Instagram and TikTok.

item.title: Gmail change may flood your inbox with political email
item.description: Gmail's Verified Sender Program launches September 8, 2026, giving U.S. political committees a more reliable path to your personal email inbox.
item.content:encoded:
If your Gmail inbox already feels crowded, election season may add another layer of noise. Starting Sept. 8, 2026, Google's new Gmail Verified Sender Program will give qualifying U.S. political committees a more reliable path to personal Gmail accounts. That means qualifying political committees will have a new way to improve the reliability of their email delivery, provided they follow Google's security, authentication and spam requirements.

The program applies to eligible candidates, parties, PACs and other registered political committees that meet Google's requirements. Campaign Verify's eligibility criteria focus on registration and program requirements, regardless of party label.

The bigger issue for you is control. You can still unsubscribe, block a sender, report unwanted messages as spam or create your own Gmail filters.

Missed CyberGuy LIVE? Watch the Protect Your Money replay

Our free CyberGuy LIVE class, Protect Your Money From Today’s Biggest Threats, has ended, but you can still watch the full replay and download our financial protection checklist. Kurt "CyberGuy" Knutsson walks you through five simple ways to help defend yourself against AI scams, fraud, identity theft and financial hacks. You’ll learn how to set up bank alerts, strengthen your account logins, protect your phone number, freeze your credit and help secure your retirement savings against unauthorized transfers. No technical experience is needed.

Get the free replay and checklist now at CyberGuyLive.com

DO NOT CLICK FAKE 'ACCOUNT RECOVERY' AMAZON EMAIL

The Gmail Verified Sender Program is scheduled to launch September 8 for eligible U.S. political committees. Campaign Verify says political organizations must verify their sending domains before they can participate. Eligible groups include candidates, parties, PACs and other political committees that qualify under the program. Google also requires participating senders to follow email security and compliance rules. One key requirement is a user-reported spam rate below 0.3% over a rolling 14-day average.

Getting verified alone does not guarantee that every campaign message will reach your inbox. Google says continued participation depends on senders following its requirements and maintaining positive recipient engagement. If a sender's average user-reported spam rate rises above 0.3% over a rolling 14-day period, the sender violates the program's policy and could be suspended or removed. Standard Gmail spam filtering would then apply.

So, this does not give campaigns unlimited access to your inbox. However, it changes how Gmail can treat eligible political email before you personally tell Gmail what you want. One more point: verification confirms the political committee's sending domain. It should not be read as Google vouching for every claim, fundraising pitch or link inside a message.

Here is the part that could get annoying. Gmail has long used automated systems to decide whether bulk email belongs in your inbox or spam folder. Under the new program, verified political senders that stay within Google's rules can receive more reliable delivery to personal Gmail accounts.

For someone who already receives fundraising appeals, petition requests or campaign updates, that could mean seeing more political messages in Gmail. Google tells CyberGuy the program grew out of an earlier pilot and says Gmail users will remain in control of what stays in their inboxes.

"Following our previous pilot, this program is designed to connect people with the emails they want to receive while keeping them fully in control of their inboxes. To participate, bulk senders must meet strict security and compliance requirements, ensuring that messages people receive are relevant, useful, and verified," a Google spokesperson told CyberGuy.

Google also points out that Gmail users can continue to mark a message as spam, block a specific sender and unsubscribe from unwanted mailing lists. The company says the new program does not turn off Gmail's broader security protections. Google says Gmail's filters continue to block more than 99.9% of spam, phishing and malware while using recipient feedback to help determine what people want to receive. Still, if more qualifying political messages reach you, some of the cleanup work may fall on you.

RUSSIAN HACKERS CAN STEAL EMAILS WITHOUT A CLICK

This is where your own Gmail choices become important. According to reporting on the new program, if you mark a participating sender's message as spam, Gmail can use that feedback for your account. Future messages from that sender can then be routed to spam based on your preference.

Google's standard Gmail tools also confirm that messages you report as spam move into the Spam folder. Over time, reporting unwanted email helps Gmail identify similar messages more effectively. In other words, do not assume you have to live with every campaign message that reaches you.

You have several ways to take back your inbox. Start with the least aggressive option and move up if the messages keep coming.

On a computer, open the message and look next to the sender's name. If Gmail shows an Unsubscribe option, click it and confirm. Google says some unsubscribe requests can take a few days to fully stop the mail. Gmail may also send you to the sender's website when a one-click option is unavailable.

If you did not ask for the message or the sender keeps emailing you after you tried to leave the list, select the email and click Report spam. That moves the message into Spam and gives Gmail another signal about what you do not want.

For a sender you never want to hear from again, Gmail lets you block that address. Future messages from a blocked sender go to Spam. Keep in mind that campaigns may use more than one sending address or domain. Blocking one address may reduce the flow without stopping every related message.

If the same sender or phrase keeps showing up, create a filter on your computer. Open Gmail, click Show search options in the search box and enter the sender, domain or other criteria you want to target. Then click Create filter and choose what Gmail should do with matching messages. You can archive them, apply a label or delete them automatically. I would be careful with broad keywords such as "vote" or "election." Those words can appear in news alerts, community messages and emails you actually want. A specific sender or domain gives you more control.

FAR-LEFT POLITICIANS STILL USING ACTBLUE AS 88-YEAR-OLD DISPUTES DONATING NEARLY $150,000 TO FUNDRAISING GIANT

Political campaigns and other organizations can obtain contact information from many sources, including public records and commercial data providers. Reducing the amount of personal information circulating online may help limit some unwanted outreach.

A personal data removal service can do much of the cleanup for you. They can send removal requests to data brokers on your behalf and continue following up as your information reappears. This can reduce your exposure across data broker and people-search sites. However, it cannot remove information from government websites, so it will not stop every political email or message.

The less personal information that data brokers have available to package and share, the fewer places marketers and other organizations may have to find your contact details. Check out my top picks for data removal services and get a free scan to find out if your personal information is already out on the web by visiting Cyberguy.com.

Political email can also give scammers an easy theme to copy. If a message pressures you to donate immediately, verify your identity or click a link before a deadline, avoid using the link in the email when anything feels off. Go directly to the campaign or organization's official website instead. CyberGuy has covered how scammers use fake political donation requests and how political messages can hide scam links.

One of the best ways to reduce future clutter is to stop handing out your main email address everywhere. An email alias gives you another address that forwards to your inbox. You can use a separate alias for donations, petitions, newsletters or other sign-ups. If that alias starts getting flooded, you can shut it down without changing your primary address. For recommendations on private and secure email providers that offer alias addresses, visit Cyberguy.com.

This Gmail change arrives at a time when many people already feel buried by junk email, spam texts, robocalls and political messages.

We covered exactly that in our free CyberGuy LIVE class, "Sick of Spam?" The live session has ended, but you can still get the replay and our spam-stopping checklist. I walk you through ways to reduce junk email, cut down robocalls, curb political texts and clean up unwanted messages. Get the free CyberGuy LIVE replay and checklist at Cyberguy.com/cyberguylive/classes/#past-classes. That is worth doing before September 8, especially if your inbox already feels like a dumping ground.

Google is giving verified political committees a new path to more reliable email delivery, but campaigns still have to play by Gmail's rules. Users also retain the power to unsubscribe, block senders and hit the spam button. From a security standpoint, verifying political senders can help make impersonation harder. From an inbox standpoint, however, you may still end up doing more of the sorting yourself if campaign volume picks up. My advice is simple: use Gmail's controls aggressively when a message keeps showing up after you have had enough. Unsubscribe from legitimate lists. Report suspicious or unwanted messages as spam. Create targeted filters for repeat senders. Then think about using an alias for future political sign-ups so your primary email stays cleaner. Google's 0.3% spam threshold also gives campaigns a strong incentive to avoid irritating recipients. The real test will come after September 8, when political email volume increases and Gmail users start voting with the Report spam button.

Would you rather Gmail make more of the initial decision about which political emails belong in spam, or are you comfortable deciding sender by sender once those messages reach you? Let us know by writing to us at CyberGuy.com.

item.title: OJ Simpson jokes about ‘bloody Bronco,’ boasts of its ‘great escapability’ in disturbing resurfaced video
item.description: Resurfaced video from O.J. Simpson's prank show "Juiced" captures him joking about a "bloody Bronco" and boasting about its "great escapability."
item.content:encoded:
O.J. Simpson turned one of the most infamous moments of his life into a punchline.

Years after the fallen football star and Hollywood actor was acquitted of the murders of his ex-wife and her friend, Simpson was caught on camera joking about a "bloody Bronco" and boasting about the vehicle’s "great escapability" — video that has now resurfaced decades later.

The moments were captured while Simpson filmed his hidden-camera prank show, "Juiced," in an attempt at a comeback. Simpson’s little-remembered project, which he described as his "own version of 'Punk’d,'" is the subject of a new Investigation Discovery docuseries, "O.J. Unseen: Exploitation of Evil."

NICOLE BROWN SIMPSON TOLD FORMER LOVER SHE'D 'RATHER DIE' THAN RETURN TO O.J. SIMPSON BEFORE HER MURDER

Simpson faced repeated allegations of domestic violence involving Nicole Brown Simpson. He pleaded no contest to a charge of spousal battery against her in 1989.

"O.J. was a malignant narcissist and megalomaniac who thought he could get away with anything — that’s what doing [this docuseries] showed me," filmmaker Rebecca Halpern told Fox News Digital.

"O.J. insisted on having a beer in his hand for virtually the entire production, and loose lips sink ships. And there are many scenes in the show where O.J. just starts to blather on about the case. Nobody prompted him to tell a shopper on a used car lot that a white Bronco has ‘great escapability’ and if you do something bad, it can get you out of trouble."

WATCH: O.J. SIMPSON DEAD AFTER CANCER BATTLE AT 76

In a scene from the docuseries, which premieres Sept. 7, Simpson pretends to sell a white Bronco at a used car lot, where he boasts about making the car famous. The Bronco appears to have a bullet hole in it.

"It was good for me," Simpson tells a prospective buyer. "Got me out of harm’s way."

When another customer jokes about whether there is "a dead body inside," Simpson replies, "Yeah, well, hopefully there’s no bodies in this thing." He also tells two other shoppers, "It’s a Bronco, a car that I personally made famous."

"This is the best deal we got on the lot," he tells another. "It has escapability, that’s the main thing. I mean, if you ever get into some trouble and you gotta get away, it has escapability. ... I like that word, escapability. ... They weren’t going to let me keep mine."

When customers realize they are being filmed for the hidden-camera prank, some laugh, shake Simpson’s hand or embrace him. At one point, he autographs the Bronco.

"This is a Bronco signed by O.J. Simpson," he says. "With an authentic bullet hole in it. It’s signed by me, which gives it some kind of extra value."

GET ENTERTAINMENT SCOOP DELIVERED RIGHT TO YOUR EMAIL BY CLICKING HERE

"I wasn’t trying to escape, despite what anybody might tell you. No, that’s the God’s truth. That’s why they never brought the Bronco ride up in any of my trials," Simpson said.

"Just take a look around. All you have to do is wash it up."

Simpson and Brown married in 1985. They had two children, Sydney and Justin, and divorced in 1992. Two years later, Brown and her friend Ronald Goldman were found stabbed to death outside her Los Angeles home.

Investigators quickly focused on Simpson, leading to a slow-speed chase in a white Bronco that aired live on national television. Following the "Trial of the Century," he was acquitted of murder.

Simpson was later found liable for the deaths in a separate civil case and served nearly nine years in prison after he was convicted of armed robbery and other charges in an unrelated Las Vegas case.

Halpern said Simpson "demonstrated such a complete and total lack of any decency" while discussing his case during filming.

LIKE WHAT YOU'RE READING? CLICK HERE FOR MORE ENTERTAINMENT NEWS

"He was so desperate for a comeback, to prove to the world that he was still this beloved figure, that he was willing to make jokes at his dead ex-wife’s expense," Halpern said. "And then, on top of that, to shock innocent victims, many of whom were female in these pranks. If that doesn’t say it all, I don’t know what does."

"There is [also] a scene at a fast-food restaurant where O.J. begins to fat shame women who are at the drive-thru," Halpern said. "We cut from that to Nicole Brown Simpson’s sister on the stand testifying about O.J. Simpson; when Nicole was pregnant with their children, he would fat shame her and call her a 'fat pig.'"

The Bronco remarks weren’t the only comments that left crew members stunned.

"When he was getting his makeup done for this crazy bingo sketch where he was playing an old White man, he starts talking about rape culture and the Kobe Bryant case while he’s watching Court TV," Halpern explained. "He goes on to say, 'No doesn’t always mean no.' Nobody prompted him to say that."

Former "Juiced" crew members participated in the docuseries, with some saying they hoped Simpson would let his guard down — and possibly confess to the murders — while the cameras were rolling.

"The whole two-week journey of making 'Juiced' was a roller-coaster ride of emotions for the crew, many of whom signed on to find out for themselves if he did it," Halpern explained.

PUT YOUR ENTERTAINMENT KNOWLEDGE TO THE TEST AND SEE HOW YOU SCORE

"Along the way, they found themselves liking him sometimes, feeling sort of under his spell. And then at other times, they were completely aghast at what they saw. In fact, the VP of 'Juiced' said it himself: 'After I shook his hand when production was over, I thought to myself, "Were these the hands that killed somebody?"'"

Simpson’s attempted comeback failed to gain traction. After word of "Juiced" leaked, distributors backed away as details emerged of Simpson joking about the murders, according to the docuseries. The project’s original distribution plans quickly collapsed. "Juiced" aired as a pay-per-view special in 2006 and was later released on DVD.

"It imploded," Halpern said. "There was a backlash on the business side that distributors and others didn’t want to have anything to do with anything O.J. Simpson joking about the murders. They all started to get cold feet. And I think [executive producer] Rick Mahr saw the writing on the wall for his project."

Simpson died of prostate cancer in 2024 at 76.

"He wanted to prove to the world that he was not the pariah that the media had made him out to be," Halpern said. "He had lost everything. He had reached rock bottom and was desperate for the love that he once had. That’s why he did 'Juiced.' I also think, take it for what it’s worth, whether he did it or not, O.J. Simpson knows a lot about what happened."

item.title: DHS chief announces changes to its seal to reflect that department is 'at war every single day'
item.description: Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin says DHS is changing its seal so the eagle faces arrows of war amid terrorism and cartel threats.
item.content:encoded:
Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin revealed on "The Sunday Briefing" that DHS is changing its seal, which depicts an eagle holding a palm leaf in one talon and a bundle of arrows in the other. The new seal will show the eagle facing toward the arrows rather than the palm, a symbolic shift Mullin said reflects the department’s daily fight against threats to the country.

Ahead of the 25th anniversary of 9/11, Mullin declared that the department is "at war every single day" against bad actors targeting the United States, from Islamic terrorists to drug cartels.

Mullin said the direction the eagle faces carries symbolic meaning, explaining that looking toward the palm represents peace while facing the arrows represents war. He tied the change to what he described as an increasingly fluid threat environment spanning terrorism, cartels, cyberattacks, drones and violence against public officials.

US COUNTERINTELLIGENCE ‘WAY BEHIND,’ POST-9/11 RECORD ‘EXTRAORDINARILY NEGLIGENT’, FMR TRUMP WH OFFICIAL WARNS

"If you look at most of our seals throughout all the agencies, the eagle looks to the palm because that's in a time of peace. We're actually changing our seal to make it look towards the arrows, because when it looks towards the arrows is when it means we're at war."

Asked about the leading threat to the homeland today, Mullin said terrorism still tops the list, but it looks different than it used to.

"It's still terrorists, but the terrorists have joined with the cartels," said Mullin, pointing out that fentanyl overdoses have killed more Americans than the Vietnam War and praising President Donald Trump for adding cartels to the list of Foreign Terrorist Organizations and Specially Designated Global Terrorists.

AMERICA'S POWER GRID, FOOD SUPPLY AND MORE ARE UNDER THREAT FROM DRONES

"We're seeing the Islamic terrorists joining with the Mexican cartels that are trying to use all the resources to come after us. And then, we're seeing the drone attacks that are starting to take place," Mullin said.

"We have tried to protect our sensitive areas with fences and armed security guards. Now we're having to realize that the threat comes from the air, too, with simple drones that people can buy online on Amazon."

Given that Labor Day serves as the traditional kickoff to campaign season, Mullin also reflected on the threats faced by political candidates.

FORMER HOUSE INTEL LEADER POINTS TO DEM RHETORIC 'ENCOURAGING' VIOLENCE; EIGHTH MAN CHARGED IN UFC TERROR PLOT

"I would say you're never safe when you're [in the] public eye," he said, calling for cooler heads to prevail.

"The American people have to realize that we do have a republic, and the republic has different opinions. And it's okay to have different opinions, just when you cross the line and say that that different opinion needs to be silenced, needs to be silenced through violence — that's where Homeland comes into place, that's where we're going to stop that violent act."

That's not to mention the new frontier of cyber threats. Mullin identified Iran, North Korea, China and Russia-linked actors as some of the main sources of today's cyberattacks, which number in the hundreds of thousands each week, according to the DHS chief.

He emphasized the importance of staying agile in the face of an ever-changing risk environment.

"Every single day, I get a briefing. Every single day we have new threats, and every single day the threats are changing," Mullin said. "Every time we stop a threat, a terrorist act or a criminal activity that's taking place, they also change their tactics. We have to be constantly moving from cyber to sea to air and to land."

item.title: Alleged cryptoscam ringleader set for plea hearing in $240M bitcoin theft
item.description: Malone Lam allegedly used a social engineering attack to steal over 4,100 Bitcoin, then blew millions on Lamborghinis, nightclubs and mansions.
item.content:encoded:
A 22-year-old Singapore man accused of helping steal more than $240 million in Bitcoin from a single victim and splurging the proceeds on luxury cars, private jets, mansions and wild nights out is expected to plead guilty this week in one of the largest cryptocurrency thefts in U.S. history.

Malone Lam, an eighth-grade dropout from Singapore whom prosecutors have identified as a suspected ringleader of the sprawling cryptocurrency scheme, is scheduled for a plea agreement hearing Tuesday in federal court in Washington, D.C.

Lam and his alleged co-conspirators were part of an alleged network of young men in their late teens and early 20s who prosecutors say used a sophisticated "social engineering" attack in August 2024 to trick a wealthy, longtime cryptocurrency investor into handing over access to his digital holdings.

GLOBAL TASK FORCE DISMANTLES 'PIG-BUTCHERING' CRYPTO FRAUD RINGS PREYING ON AMERICANS

According to prosecutors, members of the group contacted the victim while posing as representatives of Google and the Gemini cryptocurrency exchange, warning him that his accounts had been compromised.

The scammers allegedly convinced the victim to give them access to his Google Drive and provide security codes that allowed Lam and others to siphon off more than 4,100 Bitcoin, then worth over $240 million.

The group allegedly moved the stolen cryptocurrency through multiple exchange platforms and used money laundering specialists to convert portions of it into cash.

Prosecutors say Lam and his associates then embarked on a staggering spending spree.

Lam and his friends allegedly spent $4 million at Los Angeles nightclubs in roughly a month, including more than $569,000 that Lam allegedly spent during a single night out. He also allegedly used stolen cryptocurrency to purchase a $2 million watch and more than 30 vehicles, including custom Porsches, Lamborghinis and Ferraris.

The group also rented multimillion-dollar homes, flew on private jets and hired private security.

The alleged spending was so lavish that the judge overseeing Lam's initial court appearance in Miami invoked a famous Hollywood troublemaker after hearing a prosecutor describe it.

"I could only think of Ferris Bueller gone bad," U.S. Magistrate Judge Alicia Valle said, referring to the school-skipping protagonist of the 1986 movie "Ferris Bueller's Day Off."

FBI WRAPS UP CYBERCRIME OPERATION TARGETING GLOBAL NETWORKS PREYING ON AMERICANS

The lavish lifestyle quickly attracted attention as investigators closed in.

One alleged co-conspirator, Jeandiel Serrano, failed to conceal his IP address while creating an account on a cryptocurrency exchange that held nearly $30 million in stolen funds, prosecutors said. Investigators traced the address to an Encino, California, home Serrano was renting for $47,500 per month.

Serrano and Lam were arrested separately on Sept. 18, 2024. FBI agents took Serrano into custody at Los Angeles International Airport, where authorities said he was wearing a watch worth roughly $500,000.

Lam was arrested the same day at a Miami mansion.

Eighteen defendants have been charged in connection with the case, with ten already pleading guilty.

At Lam's initial court appearance, a prosecutor estimated that federal sentencing guidelines could call for a prison term of at least 14 years if he is convicted.

The Associated Press contributed to this report.
